# Clinical Intake and Patient Support Assistant - RFP Extract and Discovery Notes

## 1. Background

Harborview Health Network is a non-profit provider network of six outpatient clinics and one referral centre serving the greater Portland metro area.
Our clinics see approximately 85,000 patient encounters per month across primary care, behavioural health and physical therapy.
Referral letters, prior-authorisation forms and outside lab results arrive by fax, secure email and patient portal upload, and today a team of eleven medical records clerks manually reads and keys each document into our EHR.
Patients also call our front-desk line roughly 12,000 times per month with routine questions about appointment prep, billing and insurance coverage, most of which do not require clinical judgement.
We want a partner to build a clinical-document intake system and a patient-support assistant that reduce this manual burden while keeping every clinical decision in the hands of our staff.

## 2. Current Systems Landscape

Epic is our electronic health record system of record across all six clinics and the referral centre, exposed to partners through Epic's FHIR R4 API.
Our practice-management and scheduling data also lives in Epic and is accessible through the same FHIR interface.
Incoming documents are currently scanned into a shared network drive and manually filed by the medical records team before being keyed into Epic.
Our current phone system is a cloud contact-centre product from Five9, which front-desk staff use today for the 12,000 monthly patient calls.
A regional health information exchange, CareEverywhere, is used ad hoc by physicians to pull outside records, but is not integrated into our intake workflow.

## 3. Business Requirements

BR1. The solution must reduce the time medical records clerks spend keying referral and prior-authorisation documents into Epic by at least 50%.
BR2. The solution must reduce routine front-desk call volume by giving patients a self-service way to get appointment-prep and billing answers.
BR3. The solution should reduce the average time from document receipt to the document being visible in a patient's Epic chart.
BR4. Every clinical or coverage decision must remain with a licensed staff member; the assistant must never make an autonomous clinical or eligibility determination.
BR5. The solution could eventually extend to behavioural-health intake screening, though that is out of scope for this initial phase.

## 4. Functional Requirements

FR1. The system must accept incoming referral letters, prior-authorisation forms and lab results from fax, secure email and patient-portal upload.
FR2. The system must extract structured fields from each document, including patient identifiers, referring provider, requested service and supporting clinical notes.
FR3. The system must present each extracted document to a medical records clerk for review and correction before anything is written to Epic.
FR4. Approved documents must be written back to the correct patient chart in Epic through the FHIR R4 API, tagged with the extracting user and timestamp.
FR5. The patient-support assistant must answer common questions about appointment preparation, clinic locations, hours and accepted insurance plans.
FR6. The patient-support assistant must retrieve answers from our approved clinic policy and FAQ documents rather than generating unsourced medical guidance.
FR7. The patient-support assistant must recognise when a question requires clinical judgement or involves symptoms and must hand off to a human staff member.
FR8. The assistant must be available through our existing patient portal and, if feasible, as a widget on our public website.
FR9. Medical records clerks must be able to see a queue of documents awaiting review, prioritised by how long they have been waiting.
FR10. The system should flag documents where extraction confidence is low so clerks review those first.

## 5. Non-Functional Requirements

NFR1. The intake system must process at least 85,000 patient encounters worth of associated documents per month without a growing backlog.
NFR2. Document extraction results must be available to a reviewing clerk within 5 minutes of document receipt for 95% of documents.
NFR3. The solution must support approximately 1,200 clinical and administrative staff users plus patient-facing assistant traffic estimated at 85,000 conversations per month.
NFR4. The patient-support assistant must respond to a typical question within 4 seconds.
NFR5. The system must maintain 99.5% availability during clinic operating hours, 7am to 8pm Pacific, seven days a week.
NFR6. Every assistant answer and every extracted field must be traceable back to the source document or policy document it came from.

## 6. Integration Requirements

INT1. The intake system must integrate with Epic through the FHIR R4 API to write structured document data and retrieve patient context.
INT2. The intake system must accept inbound documents from our existing fax gateway, secure email inbox and patient-portal upload mechanism.
INT3. The patient-support assistant should integrate with Five9 so a handed-off conversation can be routed to an available front-desk agent with context preserved.
INT4. The assistant must authenticate patients through the existing patient-portal login rather than introducing a separate identity system.
INT5. The solution should be able to query the regional CareEverywhere health information exchange in a later phase, but that integration is not required for go-live.

## 7. Data Requirements

DATA1. All patient documents and extracted fields are protected health information and must be handled under our HIPAA policies at every stage.
DATA2. The assistant's knowledge base must be built only from clinic-approved policy, FAQ and appointment-prep documents, refreshed whenever those documents change.
DATA3. Extracted document data and assistant conversation logs must be retained for at least six years to satisfy state medical-records requirements.
DATA4. Conversation logs must be reviewable by compliance staff but must not be used to retrain or fine-tune any model without a separate, explicit approval process.
DATA5. Document images and extracted text must be encrypted at rest, separate from the assistant's conversational session data.

## 8. Security and Compliance

SEC1. The solution must comply with HIPAA, including a signed business associate agreement with any AI provider or subprocessor involved.
SEC2. All protected health information must be encrypted in transit and at rest using current industry-standard algorithms.
SEC3. Access to the document-review queue must be role-based and limited to authorised medical records staff, with supervisor audit visibility.
SEC4. Multi-factor authentication must be enforced for all staff accessing the intake review queue or extracted patient data.
SEC5. The solution must undergo a HIPAA security risk assessment before go-live.
SEC6. The patient-support assistant must never display another patient's information, even if a conversation is misrouted.

## 9. Technology Preferences

TECH1. Our infrastructure team runs existing workloads on Amazon Web Services and would prefer the new intake and assistant platform to run on AWS.
TECH2. We are open to a managed AI/ML service for document extraction and the assistant, as long as it can meet our HIPAA and data-handling requirements.
TECH3. Our two in-house developers have Python experience and would like to be able to maintain integration code after handover.

## 10. Delivery Constraints and Timeline

CON1. We would like a phased rollout starting with document intake within 24 weeks of contract signature, with the patient-support assistant following in a second phase.
CON2. The medical records team must be able to fall back to today's manual process at any time during the initial rollout if extraction quality is not trusted yet.
CON3. Our compliance officer must approve the assistant's response content and escalation rules before any patient-facing pilot begins.
CON4. Clinical and administrative staff can provide at most one subject-matter expert two days a week during the build; the delivery partner is expected to own the technical build.

## 11. Discovery Call Notes - 2026-09-02

Attendees: Chief Medical Information Officer, Director of Patient Access, Compliance Officer (Harborview Health Network); Engagement Manager, AI Solution Architect (delivery partner).
The Chief Medical Information Officer emphasised that clinician trust depends on every extracted field and every assistant answer being traceable to a source document.
The Compliance Officer confirmed a business associate agreement will be required with whichever AI provider is ultimately used and asked to review that agreement before any pilot.
The Director of Patient Access asked whether the assistant could eventually support Spanish-language conversations, given about 18% of patients prefer Spanish, but this was not committed to for the initial phase.
It is still unclear whether Epic's FHIR R4 API in our current sandbox environment supports writing structured referral data or only reading patient context; the CMIO will confirm with the Epic team.
No decision has been made yet on whether the assistant runs as a fully separate application or is embedded directly inside the existing patient portal.

prd.title: Clinical Intake and Patient Support Assistant - Product Requirements Document

statements.text: Harborview Health Network needs a HIPAA-compliant clinical-document intake pipeline and a retrieval-grounded patient-support assistant on AWS, integrated with Epic via FHIR R4, serving roughly 1,200 staff and 85,000 monthly patient encounters with a 24-week phased rollout; Epic sandbox write access and the assistant's deployment form remain open.
statements.label: ai-interpretation

statements.text: Clinical Intake and Patient Support Assistant serves 4 business objectives set by Harborview Health Network (BR_01, BR_02, BR_03 and BR_04); each is detailed under Business objectives.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: The solution is organised into 6 capability areas (Application Experience, Platform Foundation, Data Platform, Systems Integration, AI Capabilities and Security and Compliance) and connects to Epic EHR (SYS_01), Five9 Contact Centre (SYS_02), CareEverywhere Health Information Exchange (SYS_03) and Patient Portal (SYS_05).
statements.label: ai-interpretation

statements.text: Today Harborview Health Network relies on Manual Document Scanning Process: Incoming documents are currently scanned into a shared network drive and manually filed by the medical records team before being keyed into Epic.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: Until this is addressed, Harborview Health Network cannot achieve "Cut document-keying time by 50%" (BR_01), "Reduce routine front-desk call volume" (BR_02), "Faster document-to-chart visibility" (BR_03) and "Clinical decisions stay with licensed staff" (BR_04).
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: BR_01 - Cut document-keying time by 50%: Reduce the time medical records clerks spend keying referral and prior-authorisation documents into Epic by at least 50%.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: BR_02 - Reduce routine front-desk call volume: Reduce routine front-desk call volume by giving patients a self-service way to get appointment-prep and billing answers.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: BR_03 - Faster document-to-chart visibility: Reduce the average time from document receipt to the document being visible in a patient's Epic chart.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: BR_04 - Clinical decisions stay with licensed staff: Every clinical or coverage decision remains with a licensed staff member; the assistant never makes an autonomous clinical or eligibility determination.
statements.label: customer-requested

statements.text: PER_01 - Medical Records Clerk: One of eleven staff who manually read and key referral and prior-authorisation documents into Epic today, and who will review extracted data.
statements.label: ai-interpretation

statements.text: PER_02 - Patient: Calls or messages the clinic with appointment-prep, billing and insurance questions and will interact with the support assistant.
statements.label: ai-interpretation

statements.text: Medical Records Clerk journey: Step 1: Present each extracted document to a medical records clerk for review and correction before anything is written to Epic (FR_03; delivered by CAP_01). Step 2: Medical records clerks see a queue of documents awaiting review, prioritised by how long they have been waiting (FR_08; delivered by CAP_04). Step 3: Documents where extraction confidence is low are flagged so medical records clerks review those first (FR_10; delivered by CAP_11).
statements.label: ai-interpretation

statements.text: Patient journey: Step 1: The patient-support assistant answers common questions about appointment preparation, clinic locations, hours and accepted insurance plans (FR_05; delivered by CAP_10). Step 2: The assistant recognises when a question requires clinical judgement or involves symptoms and hands off to a human staff member (FR_07; delivered by CAP_04). Step 3: The patient-support assistant is available through the existing patient portal and, where feasible, as a widget on the public website (FR_09; delivered by CAP_03, CAP_10).
statements.label: ai-interpretation

capabilities.name: Document Management

It delivers: BR_01 (Cut document-keying time by 50%), BR_03 (Faster document-to-chart visibility), FR_01 (Multi-channel document intake), FR_03 (Mandatory clerk review before write-back), FR_04 (Approved-document write-back to Epic). Document versions and access are tracked so an auditor can reconstruct who accessed what.

acceptance: A form rejects incomplete or invalid submissions with a clear, field-level message.
A submitted form is stored in a structured shape a downstream process can consume.

summary.text: The proposed solution architecture targets Microsoft Azure and is composed of 25 components covering 14 functional capabilities. It spans the full reviewed scope; see each component’s own rationale below for its specific citations.
summary.label: ai-interpretation

components.name: Web Front End
components.service: Azure Static Web Apps with Azure Front Door
components.purpose: Serves the customer-facing web experience and delivers static assets close to users.
components.rationale: Azure Static Web Apps with Azure Front Door serves the web experience with edge caching, TLS termination and low first-byte latency worldwide. It addresses NFR_06.
tradeOffs: Edge caching improves latency but requires explicit cache-invalidation on release.
A globally distributed edge adds a small recurring data-transfer cost versus single-region hosting.
securityConsiderations: Enforce HTTPS-only delivery and a strict Content-Security-Policy at the edge.
Restrict direct access to origin storage so all traffic is served through the CDN.

components.name: API Layer
components.purpose: Exposes the solution's functional capabilities as versioned, governed APIs for the front end and integrations.
components.rationale: Azure API Management centralizes authentication, throttling and request validation ahead of the application compute runtime. It addresses NFR_01, NFR_06 and SEC_03.
tradeOffs: A managed gateway adds a small per-request latency and cost overhead versus calling services directly.
API versioning policy must be agreed early to avoid breaking existing client integrations.
securityConsiderations: Apply request-rate throttling and payload-size limits to reduce abuse and denial-of-service exposure.
Validate and authorize every request against the identity provider before it reaches the runtime.

components.name: Application Compute Runtime
components.purpose: Hosts the backend business logic that implements the reviewed functional requirements.
components.rationale: Azure Container Apps runs the backend services with managed autoscaling so capacity tracks real traffic without manual intervention. It addresses NFR_01 and NFR_06.
tradeOffs: Container-based hosting requires a build/release pipeline for every deployable service.
Autoscaling limits must be tuned against real traffic before go-live to avoid cost or latency surprises.
securityConsiderations: Run containers with least-privilege service identities and no long-lived static credentials.
Scan container images for known vulnerabilities before each release.

components.name: Primary Relational Database
components.service: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server
components.purpose: Stores the core transactional data the application reads and writes.
components.rationale: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server provides managed relational storage with automated backups, patching and encryption at rest. It addresses NFR_01, NFR_06 and SEC_02.
tradeOffs: A managed relational engine caps vertical scale; very high write throughput may need read replicas or partitioning later.
Schema migrations must be coordinated with application deployments to avoid downtime.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt data at rest and in transit, and restrict network access to the application tier only.
Apply least-privilege database roles per service rather than a single shared credential.

components.name: Customer Identity and Access Management
components.purpose: Handles registration, sign-in, session management and multi-factor authentication for end users.
components.rationale: Microsoft Entra External ID provides managed sign-up, sign-in, SSO federation and MFA so authentication is never implemented by hand. It addresses SEC_03 and SEC_04.
tradeOffs: A managed identity provider constrains custom sign-in UX to its supported customization hooks.
Federating with an external identity provider (SSO) adds a dependency on that provider’s availability.
securityConsiderations: Enforce MFA for privileged accounts and require strong password/session policies for all users.
Log every authentication and authorization decision for audit purposes.

components.name: Monitoring
components.purpose: Tracks infrastructure and application health so incidents are detected before customers report them.
components.rationale: Azure Monitor aggregates metrics and dashboards with alerting thresholds tied to the availability and performance targets. It addresses FR_09, NFR_04, SEC_03, DATA_01, SEC_01, SEC_02, SEC_05 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Alert thresholds must be tuned to avoid both alert fatigue and missed incidents.
Detailed metric retention adds a recurring storage cost proportional to system scale.
securityConsiderations: Restrict dashboard and alert access to operations and engineering roles only.

components.name: Centralized Logging
components.purpose: Centralizes application and infrastructure logs for troubleshooting and audit.
components.rationale: Azure Monitor Log Analytics aggregates structured logs from every service with a defined, policy-driven retention period. It addresses SEC_03.
tradeOffs: Centralized log retention has a direct storage cost that scales with request volume.
Log content must be scrubbed of personal or sensitive data before it is retained.
securityConsiderations: Redact personal or sensitive data from log payloads before they are written.
Restrict log access to authorized operations staff and retain an access audit trail.

components.name: CI/CD Pipeline
components.purpose: Automates build, test and release of every service into each environment.
components.rationale: Azure Pipelines runs the build/test/release pipeline consistently across development, test and production. It addresses TECH_01, TECH_02, TECH_03, CON_01, CON_02, CON_03 and CON_04.
tradeOffs: A fully automated pipeline needs an initial investment in test coverage to be trustworthy for production releases.
securityConsiderations: Require code review and passing automated security scans before a release can be promoted.
Keep deployment credentials scoped to the pipeline identity, never to individual engineers.

components.name: Infrastructure as Code
components.purpose: Defines every environment declaratively so dev/test/prod stay reproducible and auditable.
components.rationale: Azure Resource Manager (Bicep templates) provisions and updates cloud resources declaratively, so environment drift is detected instead of accumulating silently. It addresses TECH_01, TECH_02, TECH_03, CON_01, CON_02, CON_03 and CON_04.
tradeOffs: Declarative provisioning has a learning curve for teams used to manual console changes.
securityConsiderations: Store infrastructure state and variables in a controlled, access-audited location, never in source control in plain text.

components.name: Secrets Manager
components.purpose: Stores and rotates credentials, API keys and connection strings used by every service.
components.rationale: Azure Key Vault (secrets) centralizes credential storage with automatic rotation and fine-grained access policies. It addresses DATA_05, SEC_02, INT_01, INT_02, INT_03 and INT_04.
tradeOffs: Every service must be updated to fetch secrets at runtime rather than reading them from local configuration.
securityConsiderations: Grant read access to a secret only to the specific service identities that need it.
Rotate credentials on a defined schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure.

components.name: Key Management
components.purpose: Manages the encryption keys that protect data at rest across storage and database services.
components.rationale: Azure Key Vault (keys, HSM-backed) issues and rotates encryption keys with a full audit trail of every key-use event. It addresses SEC_02.
tradeOffs: Customer-managed keys add operational responsibility for key rotation and recovery policy.
securityConsiderations: Rotate keys on a defined schedule and restrict key administration to a small, audited group.

components.name: Backup
components.purpose: Protects stored data with policy-driven, regularly tested backups.
components.rationale: Azure Backup takes policy-driven, encrypted backups on a defined schedule with a tested restore procedure. It addresses NFR_04.
tradeOffs: Backup retention has a direct storage cost that scales with data volume and retention period.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt backups at rest and test restores on a regular schedule, not only after an incident.

components.name: Network Protection
components.service: Azure Virtual Network with Private Endpoints
components.purpose: Isolates backend services on a private network so they are not directly reachable from the public internet.
components.rationale: Azure Virtual Network with Private Endpoints keeps service-to-service traffic off the public internet and restricts inbound access to approved paths only. It addresses BR_01, FR_01, DATA_01, DATA_05, SEC_01, SEC_02, SEC_03, SEC_04, SEC_05 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Private networking adds configuration overhead when a new service or integration needs external connectivity.
securityConsiderations: Default to deny-all network rules and open only the specific paths a service requires.
Log and periodically review network access-control changes.

components.name: WAF / DDoS Protection
components.service: Azure Web Application Firewall with Azure DDoS Protection
components.purpose: Filters malicious inbound traffic and absorbs volumetric attacks at the edge, in front of the public entry point.
components.rationale: Azure Web Application Firewall with Azure DDoS Protection inspects inbound requests against managed and custom rule sets and mitigates volumetric attacks before they reach the application. It addresses BR_01, FR_01, DATA_01, DATA_05, SEC_01, SEC_02, SEC_03, SEC_04, SEC_05 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Rule tuning is required to avoid false positives blocking legitimate traffic.
securityConsiderations: Enable managed rule sets for common web exploits and review blocked-request logs regularly.
Alert on traffic patterns consistent with a volumetric or application-layer attack.

components.name: Integration API Management
components.purpose: Publishes governed, versioned endpoints for partner and internal system integrations, separate from the product’s own front-end API.
components.rationale: Azure API Management exposes integration endpoints with independent throttling, auth and monitoring from the customer-facing API. It addresses INT_01.
tradeOffs: Running a second managed API surface adds a small recurring cost versus reusing the front-end API layer.
securityConsiderations: Require mutual authentication (API key or mTLS) for every partner system calling this surface.

components.name: Integration Service
components.purpose: Coordinates data exchange with the external systems identified in the reviewed scope.
components.rationale: Azure Logic Apps provides managed connectors, retry and error-handling policy for each external-system integration. It addresses INT_01.
tradeOffs: Each new external system requires its own connector configuration, credential and monitoring setup.
securityConsiderations: Store integration credentials in the secrets manager and scope them per external system.

components.name: Message Queue
components.purpose: Decouples integration producers and consumers so a slow or unavailable external system does not block the application.
components.rationale: Azure Service Bus (queues) buffers integration messages with dead-letter handling so failed deliveries are retried rather than lost. It addresses INT_01.
tradeOffs: Asynchronous delivery means consumers must tolerate eventual, not immediate, consistency.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt messages in transit and at rest, and restrict queue access to the integration service identity.

components.name: Object Storage
components.purpose: Stores documents and other unstructured content referenced by the application.
components.rationale: Azure Blob Storage stores unstructured content durably with lifecycle policies and encryption at rest. It addresses BR_01, BR_03, FR_01, FR_02, FR_03, FR_04, FR_06, FR_08, FR_10, NFR_01, NFR_02, NFR_05, INT_01, INT_02, DATA_01, DATA_02, DATA_03, DATA_05, SEC_03 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Large unstructured content volumes need an explicit lifecycle/retention policy to control storage cost.
securityConsiderations: Generate time-limited access URLs rather than exposing storage buckets/containers directly.

components.name: LLM Platform
components.service: Azure OpenAI in Azure AI Foundry
components.purpose: Provides managed access to foundation models for the AI use cases identified in the reviewed scope.
components.rationale: Azure OpenAI in Azure AI Foundry gives managed, guardrailed access to foundation models so AI functionality is not built on an unmanaged model endpoint. It addresses BR_04, FR_02, FR_05, FR_06, FR_07, FR_09, FR_10, NFR_02, NFR_03, NFR_05, NFR_06, INT_03, INT_04, DATA_02, DATA_03, DATA_05, SEC_06, TECH_01 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Model responses are probabilistic; outputs affecting decisions need a human-review step (see AI solution approach).
securityConsiderations: Apply content-safety guardrails and never send unmasked personal data in a prompt without a documented basis.

components.name: Vector Search
components.purpose: Retrieves the most relevant grounding content for retrieval-augmented AI responses.
components.rationale: Azure AI Search (vector search) indexes content as embeddings so the AI assistant retrieves grounded context instead of relying on model memory alone. It addresses DATA_02.
tradeOffs: Retrieval quality depends on how the source content is chunked and kept up to date; this needs an ongoing content-ops process.
securityConsiderations: Enforce the same access controls on retrieved content as on the source documents, so retrieval cannot bypass permissions.

components.name: Document AI / OCR
components.purpose: Extracts structured text and data from scanned or unstructured source documents.
components.rationale: Azure AI Document Intelligence extracts structured text, tables and key-value pairs from source documents before they are indexed or processed. It addresses FR_02, FR_10, NFR_02, NFR_05 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Extraction accuracy varies with source document quality and may need a human-review step for low-confidence results.
securityConsiderations: Route extracted personal data through the same encryption and access controls as the rest of the data estate.

components.name: High Availability & Autoscaling
components.service: Zone-redundant Azure Container Apps environment with KEDA scale rules
components.purpose: Distributes traffic and compute capacity across multiple availability zones to sustain the required uptime.
components.rationale: Zone-redundant Azure Container Apps environment with KEDA scale rules spreads compute across multiple availability zones with automatic failover and load-based scaling. It addresses NFR_04.
tradeOffs: Multi-AZ deployment increases baseline infrastructure cost versus a single-instance deployment.
securityConsiderations: Ensure failover paths are exercised in a game-day/DR test, not only documented.

components.name: Disaster Recovery / Multi-Region
components.service: Azure Database for PostgreSQL cross-region read replica with geo-redundant backup (paired region)
components.purpose: Provides a cross-region recovery path so the service can be restored after a regional outage.
components.rationale: Azure Database for PostgreSQL cross-region read replica with geo-redundant backup (paired region) replicates critical data and configuration to a secondary region with a documented recovery time/point objective. It addresses NFR_04.
tradeOffs: A warm or hot standby region roughly doubles the infrastructure cost of the protected components.
securityConsiderations: Keep the secondary region’s access controls and encryption configuration in parity with primary.

components.name: Cache
components.purpose: Reduces database load and read latency for frequently accessed data under high concurrent usage.
components.rationale: Azure Cache for Redis serves hot read paths from memory so the relational database is not the scaling bottleneck under peak load. It addresses BR_03, NFR_01 and NFR_06.
tradeOffs: Cached data can briefly go stale after a write; time-to-live and invalidation rules must be defined per data type.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt cache traffic and avoid caching personal data beyond the minimum required time-to-live.

components.name: Workflow Orchestration
components.purpose: Coordinates multi-step approval and workflow processes that span several services.
components.rationale: Azure Durable Functions tracks each workflow step’s state durably so a partially completed process can resume after a failure. It addresses FR_04, FR_06, FR_07, FR_08, DATA_02, DATA_04, SEC_03 and SEC_04.
tradeOffs: Orchestrated workflows add operational complexity versus simple synchronous calls and need their own monitoring.

integrations.name: Epic FHIR R4 write and read integration
integrations.errorHandling: Every call to Epic EHR carries an idempotency key so a retried or duplicated request is never applied twice, and a failure that exhausts its retry budget is written to a dead-letter queue rather than left half-committed.
integrations.retry: Exponential backoff starting at 1 second and doubling to a 5-attempt ceiling for calls to Epic EHR, after which the call is routed to the dead-letter queue instead of retried forever.
integrations.monitoring: Success/failure counts and latency for calls to Epic EHR are tracked in Azure Monitor, Azure Monitor Log Analytics, with an alert routed to the delivery team when the failure rate or latency crosses its threshold.
integrations.dataSync: Epic EHR is treated as the system of record for the fields it owns; conflicting updates are resolved by last-writer-wins on the record's own timestamp, and a daily reconciliation job compares record counts between Epic EHR and the platform to surface drift instead of assuming the sync is complete.

integrations.name: Patient-portal authentication reuse
integrations.protocol: OIDC/SAML federation (browser redirect) with Patient Portal over HTTPS
integrations.authentication: User-delegated OIDC/SAML federation with Patient Portal (authorization-code flow): the signed-in user's own identity is carried through, never a machine-to-machine client-credentials grant.
integrations.errorHandling: A federation failure or expired token sends the user back to sign in again rather than granting access; an outage at Patient Portal is surfaced as a sign-in error, never a silent retry.
integrations.retry: A failed sign-in is retried by the user through a fresh redirect to Patient Portal; the platform itself never automatically retries a failed authentication.
integrations.monitoring: Sign-in success/failure counts and time-to-authenticate for Patient Portal are tracked in Azure Monitor, Azure Monitor Log Analytics, with an alert when the failure rate spikes so a broken federation is caught before it locks users out.
integrations.dataSync: Patient Portal is the identity source of truth for the signed-in user during federation; the platform stores no password or long-lived credential of its own and persists nothing beyond the session created once Patient Portal confirms the user's identity.

suggestion.explanation: The estimate inputs for Clinical Intake and Patient Support Assistant are organised into 7 workstreams and 24 scope drivers across the build phases Experience and Core Platform, Data and Integration and AI Capabilities; Discovery and Architecture, Testing and Hardening, and Deployment and Handover are added as configurable overheads. Each driver cites the reviewed requirements, capabilities, architecture components, integrations or AI use cases that justify it, and its complexity is derived from the facts named in its rationale. A capability whose reviewed requirements are all already priced by AI use-case, integration or data drivers is priced once, in those more specific workstreams, never twice; two capabilities built from the same requirements are combined into one driver. The main complexity hotspots are Document Management (DRV_01), Self-Service Portal (DRV_03), Workflow and Approvals (DRV_04), Core Platform Services (DRV_05), Cloud platform foundation and environments (DRV_09), Performance and scalability hardening (DRV_11), Epic FHIR R4 write and read integration (DRV_14), Inbound document channel integration (DRV_15), Five9 handoff integration (DRV_16), Patient-portal authentication reuse (DRV_17) and Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant: Patient-support assistant Q&A and 3 related functions (DRV_23). Security and compliance work is delivered through the named security capability in the functional scope, so no separate generic security workstream is planned; that would price the same controls twice. rules.name: Driver effort
rules.formula: driver days = baseEffort[driver type][complexity]; complexity = reviewer override ?? AI suggestion
rules.description: Each scope driver is sized from the editable base-effort table. The AI only suggests the complexity level; a reviewer override replaces it and is marked user-set. A driver without a base-effort value contributes no days, is reported as a blocked scope driver and blocks the cost of its workstream and the ROM.

rules.name: Workstream base effort and complexity
rules.formula: base days = sum(driver days); complexity = round(sum(level x driver days) / sum(driver days)), Low = 1 ... Very High = 4
rules.description: A workstream is the sum of its drivers. Its complexity is the effort-weighted average of the driver complexity levels.

rules.name: Environment uplift
rules.formula: infrastructure days x (1 + max(0, environments - baselineEnvironments) x extraEnvironmentPct / 100)
rules.description: Environments beyond the baseline add effort to infrastructure drivers only. When the number of environments is unknown, no uplift is applied, the input is listed as missing and confidence is reduced.

rules.name: Productivity factor
rules.formula: likely days = round((non-infrastructure days + uplifted infrastructure days) x productivityFactor)
rules.description: The productivity assumption scales all build effort (below 1 is faster than baseline). Likely effort is rounded to whole days.

rules.name: Overhead phases
rules.formula: phase days = round(total likely build days x pctOfBuild / 100)
rules.description: Discovery and Architecture, Testing and Hardening, and Deployment and Handover are sized as configurable percentages of the adjusted build effort and staffed with the overhead role mix.

rules.name: Workstream confidence
rules.formula: High -> Medium (Very High driver, related open gap or question, outstanding delivery dependency, missing planning input) -> Low (critical unresolved gap or question on an affected input, or a blocked calculation)
rules.description: Inputs map to workstreams by driver type: integration readiness -> integration, data volume -> data, AI data availability -> AI, expected users / environments / target regions -> infrastructure, compliance scope -> security, delivery deadline -> timeline. Every reduction is listed as a confidence limitation. Overhead phases inherit the overall confidence.

rules.name: Overall confidence
rules.formula: Low if any calculation is blocked, Low-confidence workstreams hold >= 30% of build effort, or 4 or more distinct estimation inputs are missing; Medium if any workstream is below High or any input is missing; else High
rules.description: The overall level is weighted by effort so that one small uncertain workstream does not dominate, while blocked calculations and a largely unspecified engagement always do.

rules.name: Effort range
rules.formula: low = round(likely x (1 - lowPct / 100)); high = round(likely x (1 + highPct / 100))
rules.description: The range width comes from the confidence-spread table, so lower confidence widens the range instead of presenting unsupported precision. Totals are the sums of the workstream ranges.

rules.name: Role allocation
rules.formula: role days = likely days x sum(driver-type days x role mix share) / sum(driver-type days), in tenths of a day (largest remainder)
rules.description: Likely effort is split across roles with the role mix of each driver type, weighted by that type's days. Role days always add up exactly to the likely effort.

rules.name: Workstream cost
rules.formula: cost = sum(role days x role day rate); range = cost x (1 - lowPct / 100) .. cost x (1 + highPct / 100)
rules.description: A role with allocated days but no day rate, effort without a role mix, or a driver without base effort blocks the workstream cost and the ROM totals. No default rate is ever substituted.

rules.name: ROM commercials
rules.formula: subtotal = roundToUnit(sum(workstream cost)); contingency = roundToUnit(subtotal x contingencyPct / 100); ROM = subtotal + contingency
rules.description: Low, likely and high values are each rounded to the configured rounding unit and reported in the configured currency.

rules.name: Timeline
rules.formula: capacity = teamSize x workingDaysPerWeek; weeks = ceil(effort / capacity); build window = ceil(sum(build phase effort) / capacity)
rules.description: Discovery runs first; the build phases run concurrently and share the team; Testing and Hardening may overlap the last 25% of the build window but always keeps at least one week after it; Deployment and Handover runs last. The range applies the timeline confidence spread, rounded up to whole weeks.

rules.name: Deadline assessment
rules.formula: compare likely and high timeline weeks with deliveryDeadlineWeeks; required team = smallest team size whose likely timeline <= deadline
rules.description: When no deadline is configured the assessment says so, the deadline is listed as a missing input and timeline confidence is reduced.

rules.name: Missing inputs
rules.formula: missing planning input -> confidence reduced; missing day rate, role mix or base effort -> calculation blocked
rules.description: Each missing input names the affected workstreams or estimate components, the related scope items and how to resolve it. An input held open by a gap or question is never dropped: without a workstream of its driver type it affects the workstreams that share requirements with the open item, otherwise the overall estimate.

rules.name: Historical references
rules.description: Illustrative historical delivery references (sample data, not actual Topcoder records) are displayed for context only and are never an input to any rule above.

result.deadlineAssessment: The 24-week deadline is achievable at the likely timeline of 19 weeks, but the high end of the range (25 weeks) would miss it by 1 week; protect the critical path and resolve the open inputs early. The configured team of 6 is sufficient; the smallest average team that still meets the deadline at the likely effort is 5.
result.explanation: The estimate inputs for Clinical Intake and Patient Support Assistant are organised into 7 workstreams and 24 scope drivers across the build phases Experience and Core Platform, Data and Integration and AI Capabilities; Discovery and Architecture, Testing and Hardening, and Deployment and Handover are added as configurable overheads. Each driver cites the reviewed requirements, capabilities, architecture components, integrations or AI use cases that justify it, and its complexity is derived from the facts named in its rationale. A capability whose reviewed requirements are all already priced by AI use-case, integration or data drivers is priced once, in those more specific workstreams, never twice; two capabilities built from the same requirements are combined into one driver. The main complexity hotspots are Document Management (DRV_01), Self-Service Portal (DRV_03), Workflow and Approvals (DRV_04), Core Platform Services (DRV_05), Cloud platform foundation and environments (DRV_09), Performance and scalability hardening (DRV_11), Epic FHIR R4 write and read integration (DRV_14), Inbound document channel integration (DRV_15), Five9 handoff integration (DRV_16), Patient-portal authentication reuse (DRV_17) and Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant: Patient-support assistant Q&A and 3 related functions (DRV_23). Security and compliance work is delivered through the named security capability in the functional scope, so no separate generic security workstream is planned; that would price the same controls twice. Only complexity levels are suggested here: effort, timeline and ROM values are calculated from the base-effort table, role mix, day rates, contingency and team size in the estimation configuration. Calculated effort is 486 to 753 person-days (likely 573) over 17 to 25 weeks (likely 19) with Medium overall confidence. The ROM commercial range is 455,000 USD to 706,000 USD (likely 538,000 USD) including 15% contingency. Every figure is produced by the documented calculation rules CR_01 to CR_15 from the visible drivers and configuration; none is generated by the AI.
